reading.body:
HBM supply for AI training is effectively a two-supplier market, with SK Hynix as the primary partner for NVIDIA's datacenter GPUs and Micron as the only US-based alternative, both currently shipping HBM3E with HBM4 on the near horizon.

That concentration matters because HBM is not a peripheral component. It sits directly on the GPU die, and its bandwidth determines how fast a training run can move weights and activations. A cluster's compute ceiling is therefore partly a function of how much HBM those two manufacturers can produce and allocate, making memory fabrication a physical constraint on AI scaling that sits alongside power and buildings.

The storage layer recorded here is thinner in coverage: two software-defined platforms, VAST Data and WEKA, handling the I/O between persistent storage and GPU memory during training. Both are deployed at scale in GPU clusters, which signals that the filesystem tier is no longer a commodity concern, but the data does not quantify throughput requirements, deployment counts, or how storage I/O constrains training time. Standard DRAM, which the page's description mentions, has no entries here, so the picture of the full memory hierarchy is incomplete.
